newsitem.title: USA: House funds probers battle over chairman's power.
newsitem.headline: House funds probers battle over chairman's power.

text.p: The House committee investigating campaign funds abuses voted Thursday to give its chairman powers that Democrats angrily attacked as setting the stage for a one-man "witch hunt" against President Clinton's party.

The Republican-controlled committee rejected along party lines attempts by Democrats to limit the power of chairman Dan Burton, an Indiana Republican, to issue subpoenas by himself without votes by the committee or agreement by the ranking Democratic member.
"If you want to continue going down the road of this witch hunt, then grab your brooms and keep going," shouted an angry Representative Thomas Barrett, a Wisconsin Democrat.

During a lengthy, acrimonious meeting to discuss the scope and rules of the investigation, Democrats complained that Burton was being handed powers on subpoenas and given authority to release documents that other committees did not have.
Ranking Democrat Henry Waxman of California said the committee rules "would give chairman Burton unprecedented power that no one has ever had."
"This is an investigation by this committee, not chairman Dan Burton," Waxman said heatedly.

Burton issued 101 subpoenas on his own in the sweeping investigation of whether foreign funds were solicited illegally for the Democratic campaign of Clinton in the 1996 election, subpoenas issued in contemplation of future hearings.
"Power should not be concentrated in one individual," said Waxman. "Power corrupts. Absolute power corrupts absolutely."
Burton rejected charges he was being given unusual powers and said his Republican predecessor had similar authority, but Democrats disputed this.
Democrats also cried "gag rule" when debate was cut off on a Waxman amendment to require that Burton share subpoena power to give the investigation a bipartisan tone.
But Republicans defeated the Waxman plan, and another similar amendment, and authorised Burton the authority he sought.

Democratic Representative Thomas Allen of Maine said that the broad subpoenas for documents, including telephone records from Air Force One used by Clinton, and from the Democratic Party leaves "the impression one party is rummaging around in the files of the other party for partisan purposes."
Burton promised he would act fairly and consult with Democrats.
He also contended that the investigation has been "significantly hampered" because three people refused on constitutional fifth amendment grounds against self-incrimination to turn over documents.

Burton said this refusal by former Associate Attorney General Webster Hubbell, former White House aide Mark Middleton and former Democratic Party fundraiser John Huang, has caused additional work for the investigators.
Besides the House committee, campaign funds investigations are under way by a Senate committee and by a Justice Department force of 31 FBI agents.
